text.p: A troublesome power generator aboard Columbia, which threatens to end the shuttle's 16-day mission early, appeared to have stabilised, the U.S. space agency said on Sunday.
Rewiring the shuttle power systems and reducing the load on the malfunctioning fuel cell appeared to have slowed the degradation, mission control commentator Ed Campion said.
"For the time being, there's at least a somewhat more positive feeling the fuel cell is operating in a stable manner and we're just going to continue to evaluate its performance," he said.

Flight controllers were continuing to draw up plans to end the mission early if necessary, Campion said. Mission managers were to meet at mission control in Houston at about 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) to discuss the problem.

Switching off the electricity generator, one of three aboard Columbia, would force NASA to bring the shuttle home on Tuesday afternoon. The shuttle can land safely on two working fuel cells and could probably limp home on one if necessary.
The performance of the fuel cell had been degrading since the shuttle was launched on Friday. It had briefly shown signs of trouble before blastoff, but NASA thought it was working properly.
If the fuel cell degrades much more there is a danger it could catch fire or explode, NASA officials had said.

The devices, which are located in the shuttle's fuselage, provide all of the shuttle's electrical power. They combine supercold liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to generate electricity and drinking water as a byproduct.
Columbia's crew of seven was to spend 16 days in space working in a laboratory mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay. The research would come to an immediate halt if the power generator failed.
The astronauts were conducting 33 major experiments, including investigations into the behaviour of fire in space and the growth of protein crystals for medical research.

Technical problems have cut short only two previous shuttle missions. A fuel cell was to blame for bringing home early NASA's second shuttle flight in November 1981 and a failed navigation device ended a 1991 mission prematurely.
